This significant variability can be observed in Figure 11. Crucible interactions or wetting behavior, stray oxygen content in the experiment atmosphere, sample mass, sample thermal conductivity, and initial material form all alter observations. These factors would tend to decrease the observed melting enthalpy relative to the reference value. Since oxidation here is exothermic and the melting reaction is endothermic, the remaining cause for a positive deviation in melting enthalpy, in this case, would stem not from a material consideration but instead from random errors of which baseline construction would be prominent (see the single point for tin). It is for these reasons that although the absolute enthalpies may exhibit considerably more scatter, the experiment can be performed in a manner that lends itself to semi-quantitative observation. All of the uranium-based alloys are very similar masses and nominally the same dimensions, removing several of the confounding factors. Since the thermal diffusivities of the samples are reasonably close together (see thermal diffusivity section), the largest factor is likely the relatively large size of the samples which can result in a more significant temperature gradient during melting and solidification (Sánchez-Rodríguez et al. 2014). Most of the samples were very close to 2 mm thick (±0.05 mm typical). One U sample with a thickness of 1 mm was run and the observed normalized enthalpy was nearly twice that of the rest of the samples. This leads us to a major correction based on the sample size rather than with temperature. A secondary, but still important consideration is corrosion of the sample due to oxygen. While we have little recourse regarding a correction during a particular melting step, we can use only the first melting run since it will be the most accurate in terms of the mass of metallic uranium.
